terms.definition: values measured at regular times and kept in time order, e.g. one rail-rider count per day.
predicting future values, e.g. tomorrow's rail riders from the past 8 weeks.
a list of values where the order matters: 56 days of ridership, or the words of a sentence.
one position in a sequence; in our data one day. Step t means "now", step t−1 the step before.
how many people rode, counted per day: the Chicago bus and rail boardings used in this chapter.
the data's label for each date: W = weekday, A = Saturday, U = Sunday or holiday.
a pattern that repeats at a fixed interval, e.g. every week (low on Sundays) or every year.
a slow drift of a series up or down over months or years.
how many steps back you look; a 7-day lag is the value from exactly one week earlier.
the cheapest forecast: copy a past value, here the same day one week earlier.
mean absolute percentage error: each miss divided by that day's real value, signs dropped, then averaged.
mean squared error: square each miss, then average, so one big miss counts much more than several small ones.
replacing each value by (value − the value k steps earlier), which removes a repeating pattern or a drift.
a series whose average and spread stay the same over time; the opposite is non-stationary.
growing like the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 …
a formula made of powers of one quantity, such as 3t² + 2t + 1; a straight line and a quadratic are both polynomials.
a classical forecasting formula: tomorrow = weighted sum of recent real values + weighted sum of recent forecast mistakes (b04).
predicting a series from its own past values (the AR half of ARMA).
in ARMA, a weighted sum of the last q forecast mistakes. Not the everyday rolling average of values.
ARMA run on a differenced series; the I stands for the differencing.
ARIMA plus a second, seasonal copy of itself that works at the season's lag (7 days here).
a Python library of classical statistics tools (b04 uses it).
a score (AIC or BIC) that rewards fitting the data and punishes extra parameters; lower is better.
how strongly a series is correlated with itself shifted by k steps; plotting it shows which lags matter.
one value per time step, e.g. rail riders only.
several values per time step, e.g. bus AND rail riders on each day. (ch02's "multivariate" meant several OUTPUTS; here it means several inputs.)
two series that tend to rise and fall together, like bus and rail riders.
a model built from many small parts (neurons) arranged in layers; each part does a little arithmetic and passes its result on.
one small part of a neural network: it multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up plus a bias, and passes the sum through an activation function.
a number the network learns, one per connection: an input is multiplied by its weight, so the weight says how much that input counts.
in a neural network, a learned number added to a neuron's weighted sum. (Not ch02's "sampling bias".)
a fixed curve applied to a neuron's sum before it is passed on (e.g. tanh); it lets the network learn curved, nonlinear patterns.
a group of neurons that all read the same inputs; a network is several layers, each feeding the next.
a neural network where data flows one way, from inputs through the layers to the output, with no loops.
looping back: a recurrent neuron's output at one time step is fed back in as an extra input at the next step.
recurrent neural network: a neural network with recurrent neurons, so it can carry information from earlier time steps.
temporal = about time; a temporal dependency is a pattern that depends on the order of the steps and how far apart they are.
drawing a recurrent network once per time step, side by side, so the loop becomes a chain; it is still ONE set of weights.
a grid of numbers in rows and columns; 2 rows × 3 columns is a 2 × 3 matrix.
a matrix flipped on its side: rows become columns.
a small group of instances (here 32 windows) that the network processes together in one training step.
a group of windows handed to the model together, e.g. 32. (Not ch02's "batch learning".)
join two tables of numbers side by side, or one above the other.
graphics processing unit: a chip built to do many multiplications at once, which makes training much faster.
the part of a recurrent layer that does ONE time step of work and keeps a memory (its state) for the next step.
the numbers a recurrent cell carries from one time step to the next: its memory. Also called the hidden state.
a network that reads a sequence and outputs a sequence, one output per step.
a network that reads a sequence and keeps only its last output: one answer for the whole sequence.
a network that reads one input and outputs a sequence.
two networks chained: the encoder reads the whole input sequence into one vector, the decoder turns that vector into the output sequence.
whether a text is positive or negative, e.g. a film review.
an activation that returns its input unchanged.
the activation max(0, sum): negative sums become 0, positive ones pass through; it has no upper limit.
long short-term memory: a recurrent cell with a second, separate memory that is rarely overwritten, so it can learn patterns spanning many more steps (b12).
gated recurrent unit: a simpler cousin of the LSTM cell with fewer parameters (b13).
the one number that says how wrong the predictions are; training changes the weights to make it smaller.
Google's Python library for building and training neural networks in a few lines.
the larger Google library that Keras is part of; code calls it as tf, as in tf.keras.
how a neural network learns: run the data forward, measure the loss, then pass the error backward through the network to find each weight's gradient.
for one weight: how much the loss would change if that weight were nudged up a little, and in which direction.
the training method: again and again, move every weight a small step in the direction that lowers the loss.
running inputs through the network, layer by layer, to get its predictions.
backpropagation through time: unroll the RNN over the time steps, then run ordinary backpropagation on the chain.
directed acyclic graph: steps connected by arrows with no loops, like a pipeline's task graph.
the list of steps a database works out before it runs a query.
the language used to query tables in a database (SELECT … FROM …).
an SQL function that computes, for each row, a value from nearby rows (e.g. LAG() reads the row 7 back); the window frame is which rows it may see.
an SQL query that repeats itself: it starts from a first "seed" row, and each pass reads the rows the previous pass produced.
a table with one row per event or per day and number columns (measures), e.g. one row per date.
a lookup table of descriptions (e.g. a date table saying which days are holidays) that is joined onto a fact table.
an SQL statement that updates matching rows and inserts the new ones in one go.
one slice of a big table or job that is stored or processed on its own.
a fixed-length slice of consecutive values, e.g. 56 days; each window is one training instance, paired with the value that follows it.
TensorFlow's array: numbers with a fixed shape, e.g. [32, 56, 1].
the size of an array along each axis: [32, 56, 5] = 32 windows, 56 time steps, 5 numbers per step.
TensorFlow's tool for feeding data to training: a Dataset object hands out the windows batch by batch.
put the rows in a random order.
independent and identically distributed: the rows are unrelated to each other and all come from the same distribution, as gradient descent assumes.
one full pass of training over every training window.
Keras's basic recurrent layer: one state vector, rewritten at every time step.
the hyperbolic tangent, an S-shaped activation whose output always stays between −1 and +1.
an ordinary (fully connected) layer: every input feeds every neuron. (ch02's "dense" was about storing every cell of a table.)
Keras's word for a neuron: a layer with 32 units has 32 neurons.
the algorithm that changes the weights using the gradients, e.g. SGD.
stochastic gradient descent: gradient descent that updates the weights after every mini-batch.
how big each weight update is: too big and training blows up, too small and it crawls.
an optimizer option that carries part of the previous update into the next, smoothing a noisy path.
in Keras, fix the loss, optimizer and metrics of a model before training it.
a loss that acts like MSE for small errors and like MAE for large ones.
a number that scores predictions, e.g. MAE or MAPE. Keras reports metrics during training, but training does not try to lower them directly.
the MAE measured on the validation windows (January–May 2019), never used for training.
a Keras recurrent-layer option: True = output the numbers of EVERY time step (a sequence); False, the default = only the last step's.
stop training when the validation score has not improved for a while (50 epochs here) and keep the best weights.
an RNN with several recurrent layers stacked on top of each other.
a neural network with many layers; deep learning means using such networks.
put things one on top of another; stacked layers each feed the next one up.
one model trained to predict several targets at once, here bus and rail.
forecasting many days by predicting one day, appending the guess to the input, and predicting again.
how far ahead a forecast reaches: 14 days here.
a model is causal if each output uses only the current and past inputs, never later ones.
using a trained model to make predictions (as opposed to training it).
a Keras wrapper that applies the same layer separately at every time step.
gradients that grow huge (explode) or shrink to nearly 0 (vanish) as they are passed back through many steps, so training breaks.
an activation saturates when it flattens out at its limits: tanh never goes past ±1, however big its input.
cap every gradient at a maximum size so one huge gradient cannot wreck training.
rescale numbers to a common, small range, e.g. divide riders by 1,000,000, or shift and scale them to average 0 and typical size 1.
normalization using averages taken across the whole batch.
normalization using the numbers of ONE instance at ONE time step, so it works the same at every step.
during training, randomly set a fraction of values to 0 at each step so the model cannot lean on any single one.
Monte Carlo dropout: keep dropout on when predicting and predict several times; the spread of the answers shows how unsure the model is.
a range drawn around a prediction to show how unsure it is.
in Python, a blueprint for objects: it lists the data an object holds and the functions (methods) it can run.
the class a new class is built from; super().__init__() runs the parent's own setup code.
**kwargs collects any extra named arguments so they can be passed on unchanged.
a research paper posted online (arXiv is the main free site) before or instead of a journal.
inside a cell, a small layer whose outputs lie between 0 and 1; multiplying by it lets a value through (1) or blocks it (0).
the S-shaped curve (also called sigmoid) that turns any number into a number between 0 and 1.
the LSTM gate that decides which parts of the long-term memory to erase.
the LSTM gate that decides which new values are written into the long-term memory.
the LSTM gate that decides which parts of the long-term memory are read out as the output.
the LSTM's second memory, c, passed from step to step almost untouched.
the LSTM's h: its output at each step, also passed to the next step.
a proposed new memory value, which a gate may or may not let in.
the GRU gate z that decides how much old memory to keep; the new value gets the rest.
the GRU gate r that decides how much old memory the candidate is allowed to see.
a running average where each new value gets a fixed share and older values fade away.
a shortcut that adds a layer's input straight to its output, so a signal can skip past the layer (also called a skip connection).
a mechanism (Chapter 16) that lets a model look back directly at any earlier step instead of squeezing everything into one state.
a network made of attention layers instead of recurrent ones (Chapter 16). Not ch02's Scikit-Learn transformer.
a layer that slides a small learned pattern-detector along the data and records how well it matches at each position (b14).
in a convolutional layer, a small set of learned weights (e.g. 4 in a row) that detects one short pattern.
the width of a convolution filter: how many consecutive steps it looks at. (Not ch02's similarity kernel.)
the output of one filter: one number per position saying how strongly its pattern matched there.
how many steps a filter jumps between two positions; stride 2 halves the length of the output.
filler values (zeros) added at the ends of a sequence before a convolutional layer slides along it; "same" adds enough to keep the length, "valid" adds none.
keep fewer steps, e.g. every second one, making a sequence shorter.
a layer that shrinks a sequence by keeping, say, the maximum or the average of every few steps.
the span of original time steps that one output value depends on.
a 2016 network from DeepMind (Google's AI lab) made only of stacked convolutional layers whose inputs are spaced further apart at each level; used here for forecasting.
how far apart the two inputs of a filter are: rate 4 reads steps t and t−4.
padding only at the start, so no output can see a later step.
WaveNet's gate: one tanh output multiplied by one logistic output.
a free collection of ready-made datasets that load into TensorFlow in one line.
a dataset of millions of quick drawings, each stored as a sequence of pen strokes.
382 hymns by J. S. Bach, stored as sequences of 4-note chords.
the narrowest point that everything has to pass through; here, the single vector between an encoder and a decoder.
a program that runs all the time and processes data as it arrives, a little at a time.
updating a table by adding only the new rows on each run.
reading every row of a table.
what one row of a table stands for, e.g. one row per day or one row per hour.
summing detailed rows into fewer, coarser rows before an expensive step runs.
the best possible weights: where the loss is lowest.
the starting values given to a network's weights (or state) before training changes them.
one of the numbers at each time step: one per input column, or one per filter after a convolutional layer.
a single number, not a list of numbers.
guessing a value BETWEEN known ones, which is easier than forecasting one that comes after them all.
an output activation for picking one of several classes: it turns the last layer's numbers into probabilities, one per class, that add up to 1.
a 2D convolutional neural network: convolutional layers whose filters slide across an image's width and height (its spatial dimensions) rather than along time; Chapter 14 teaches them.
